title: Dealing With Conflict
coreMove: Before escalating, identify the game being played, the response your move invites, the authority structure, and whether the smarter move is to reframe or refuse the fight.
sourcePressure: The source uses game theory, authority, and loss leader strategy to frame conflict as strategic interaction where incentives, legitimacy, and selective engagement matter.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Turning conflict models into manipulative tactics or a mandate to win every visible point.

sourceAnchors.name: game theory
sourceAnchors.detail: the source supports treating conflict as strategic interaction where other people have incentives, responses, and counter-moves
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The moment the other side can answer back, your move is not a speech anymore; it is part of a game.

sourceAnchors.name: authority
sourceAnchors.detail: the source supports the role of status, credibility, and perceived legitimacy in shaping compliance or persuasion
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The same sentence changes weight when the room treats one speaker as legitimate and another as noise.

sourceAnchors.name: loss leader strategy
sourceAnchors.detail: the source supports giving ground in one place to change the larger strategic position or avoid the wrong fight
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Sometimes the visible point is cheap enough to let go because the larger game is where the real cost lives.

counterintuition: More force is not better strategy
tryThisNow: Ask what game you are in

exampleSpecs.domain: Laura, a newsroom section editor deciding whether to correct a senior columnist in the open Slack thread or move the exchange private
exampleSpecs.stakes: a public correction could harden the columnist and derail the story deadline
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Laura names the response loop, drafts a private note, and preserves the story correction without turning it into a status contest
exampleSpecs.firstImage: “If I post this here, what game starts?”
mustAvoid: public bait example from old draft

exampleSpecs.domain: Henrik, a neighborhood hockey referee handling two coaches who both want the next penalty call
exampleSpecs.audience: people mediating disputes where authority is fragile
exampleSpecs.stakes: one inconsistent signal can make the whole rink ignore him
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Henrik skates to the boards, uses the same short explanation for both benches, and protects legitimacy by refusing side arguments
exampleSpecs.firstImage: skate spray taps the boards while both benches lean forward

exampleSpecs.domain: Isabel, a co-op board treasurer deciding whether to fight a resident’s accusation line by line or publish the repair invoices plainly
exampleSpecs.stakes: a direct fight could make the accusation the main event
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Isabel gives up the satisfaction of rebutting every sentence and posts the invoices with a narrow meeting agenda
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Isabel three drafts to delete the paragraph that felt best to write

exampleSpecs.domain: Ben, a film-set assistant director de-escalating a clash between lighting and sound before the crew loses the location
exampleSpecs.stakes: winning the blame argument costs the last hour of permitted shooting
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ben reframes the fight around the location deadline, gives each department one concession, and moves the crew back to the shot
exampleSpecs.firstImage: the location permit is clipped to a sandbag beside a dying battery pack

exampleSpecs.domain: Kasia, a graduate seminar participant choosing not to crush a weak comment because it would silence the room she needs to learn from
exampleSpecs.audience: students and experts tempted to win small intellectual contests
exampleSpecs.stakes: a visible win could reduce later candor in the seminar
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Kasia writes the correction in her margin, asks a clarifying question instead, and keeps the room open for the larger discussion
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You can feel the perfect correction forming before the speaker reaches the period

exampleSpecs.domain: Hadiya, a community clinic nurse negotiating with a supplier after missed vaccine-fridge deliveries
exampleSpecs.audience: frontline professionals balancing firmness and future dependence
exampleSpecs.stakes: the clinic needs reliability without destroying a supplier relationship it still depends on
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Hadiya maps the supplier’s incentives, uses the clinic’s purchasing authority carefully, and asks for a delivery-confirmation change instead of just threatening to leave
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 7:30 a.m., Hadiya photographs the empty vaccine-fridge shelf before calling the supplier

tryThisNowSpec: Before your next reply in a live disagreement, write the response your reply is likely to invite. If that response worsens the game, choose a narrower channel, a different messenger, or no engagement.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

skillTargets: identify the chapter-specific model in a fresh scenario for Dealing With Conflict
choose the visible action that performs the core move rather than naming the concept
explain the failure mode that appears when the model is used generically
evaluate tradeoffs and limits without sliding into certainty, cynicism, or manipulation
